title: Thanks to the Judge Who Remembers
overview: The writer thanks God for defeating enemies and trusts him as a fair judge who never forgets the poor and oppressed.

parts.label: Wholehearted thanks (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The writer, traditionally David, promises full-hearted thanks and to tell others what God has done. Many scholars think Psalms 9 and 10 were first one poem whose lines began with letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, and some ancient translations join them.

parts.label: Enemies defeated (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: The writer pictures God as a judge on a throne who ruled in his favor, turning back hostile nations, probably neighboring peoples at war with Israel. The language is openly about total destruction: blotting out a name meant ruin so complete that even the memory of a people and its cities is gone.

parts.label: A judge who shelters the weak (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: Ruined cities vanish, but God's rule lasts forever, and he is a safe fortress for the oppressed when trouble comes. Zion was the hill in Jerusalem seen as God's royal seat, and calling God the one who avenges bloodshed means he holds killers to account and does not forget innocent lives taken.

parts.label: From death's gates to Zion's (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: The gates of death picture someone standing at death's doorway. City gates were also public gathering places, so the writer asks to be rescued in order to praise God openly in Jerusalem.

parts.label: Traps that backfire (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: The wicked fall into the very pits and nets they set for others, which the writer sees as God's justice at work. The Hebrew notes here, Higgaion and Selah, probably mark a solemn pause, though their exact meaning is uncertain, and the section contrasts nations that forget God with a God who never forgets the needy.

parts.label: A call for God to act (vv. 19-20)
parts.note: The writer asks God to rise up and judge the nations so that proud humans do not win. The aim is to shake them into realizing they are only mortal.

think: When people who have been badly wronged long for those who hurt them to be brought down, what do you think that longing reveals about our sense of justice?
